cards.back: The spread of observations around their mean in a sample or population model.
The uncertainty scale of an estimator across repeated samples; for a mean, approximately s/√n under independence.
The precisely defined quantity a study aims to estimate, such as a treatment effect in a target population.
A quantitative measure of the magnitude of a difference or association.
Probability under a specified null model of data at least as extreme as observed, subject to the test assumptions.
The expected fraction of false positives among rejected hypotheses under a specified multiple-testing procedure.
Treating non-independent subsamples as independent experimental replicates.
Grouping experimental units by a nuisance factor so treatment comparisons are made within more homogeneous groups.

cards.front: The vehicle mean is 10.0 μM and the compound mean is 14.0 μM. What is the compound-minus-vehicle sample contrast?
cards.back: The observed contrast is +4.0 μM. It summarizes the two samples; it does not imply that every compound replicate was higher.

cards.front: Why are two group means alone insufficient to establish statistical uncertainty or causation?
cards.back: Uncertainty needs replicate-level variability and dependence information. Causal interpretation also needs assignment details; the means alone provide neither.

cards.front: What information is lost when a graph shows group means without replicate values or uncertainty intervals?
cards.back: The mean-only plot hides within-group spread and the precision of each estimate; it cannot by itself show sampling uncertainty or establish a causal effect.
A censored subject was event-free for the time observed; keep them in the risk set until censoring and do not count an event.
S(t) is the product of (1 − d/n) over event times up to t, with n the number at risk just before each event.
Events per person-time ratio estimates a hazard ratio if hazards are roughly constant; a single HR misleads when curves cross.
If subjects leave because of the outcome, censoring is informative and the estimate is biased; report why subjects were censored.
FWER = 1 − (1 − α)ᵐ for independent tests; 20 tests at 0.05 give about 0.64.
Test each at α/m; controls FWER under any dependence; conservative for large m.
Largest i with p₍ᵢ₎ ≤ (i/m)q; reject ranks 1..i; controls FDR.
Expected fraction of false discoveries, not a per-hit probability; correct for every test run.
Difference ± t × SE; SE = s√(2/n) for equal groups; wide intervals mean imprecision, not absence.
Cohen's d = difference/SD; report raw units too.
SE ∝ 1/√n: quadrupling n halves SE; large n can make trivial effects significant.
E[x₂|x₁] = μ + r(x₁ − μ); use randomized controls selected the same way.
Biological (between units, σ_b) is what a population conclusion needs; technical (σ_t) is error on re-measuring the same unit.
Var(mean) = σ_b²/n + σ_t²/(n k): extra readings per unit shrink only the technical term; extra units shrink both.
ICC = σ_b²/(σ_b² + σ_t²); DEFF = 1 + (k − 1) ICC; effective n = N/DEFF; treating readings as independent is pseudoreplication.
SD of paired differences = √2 × σ_t; estimate it from repeated measurements of the same unit.
SE = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂); t = difference/SE; df from the Welch formula, slightly below n₁ + n₂ − 2.
A 95% interval that barely includes zero goes with p just above 0.05; the interval also shows how large the effect could be.
Analyze the within-unit differences: SE = s_d/√n, df = n − 1; pairing helps in proportion to the correlation between the measurements.
Independent units, roughly normal sampling distributions of means, outliers checked, analysis chosen in advance.
Probability of a significant result for a stated true effect; depends on δ/SE, the critical value and the number of independent units.
n per group = 2(z₁₋α/₂ + z₁₋β)² σ²/δ²; halving δ or doubling σ quadruples n; the normal formula is optimistic for small n.
Only differences above t_crit × SE are significant, so significant estimates from small studies overstate the truth.
With low power a non-significant result is inconclusive; read the interval, not the verdict.
b = S_xy/S_xx; a = ȳ − b x̄; s = √(SSE/(n − 2)); R² = 1 − SSE/SST; SE(b) = s/√S_xx.
x̂ = (y − a)/b; its uncertainty includes the new reading's scatter and the line's uncertainty, and grows away from x̄.
Plot residuals against x or the fitted value: curvature, funnels and outliers show what R² hides.
Do not extrapolate beyond the data; watch leverage; an observational slope is an association.
Under no effect, labels are exchangeable: p = (number of arrangements at least as extreme)/(total); C(8,4) = 70 arrangements for 4 + 4.
Resample the independent units with replacement; an observation appears with probability 1 − (1 − 1/n)ⁿ, about 63% for large n.
Rank the combined sample; compare rank sums; U counts pairs where one group's value exceeds the other's; report an effect estimate too.
Permute or resample the independent units; technical replicates do not count.
Average the technical readings within each animal; the animal means are the observations and the number of animals is the sample size.
Pool each animal's sum of squares about its own mean over animals × (readings − 1) degrees of freedom.
ICC = σ_b²/(σ_b² + σ_t²), where σ_b² = (MS animals − MS within)/readings; a high ICC means readings of one animal are nearly redundant.
Treating readings as independent shrinks the standard error and the p-value; compare the reading-level and animal-level tests.
PPV = true positives/(true positives + false positives); for a rare condition a positive result from a good test is often a false alarm.
LR⁺ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity); posterior odds = prior odds × LR⁺.
PPV = power π/(power π + α(1 − π)); low power or a low prior makes many significant results false.
P(significant replication) = PPV × power + (1 − PPV) × α; a failed replication of an underpowered result is common.

cards.front: Chance of a hit among many
cards.back: With k independent null tests the chance of at least one p < 0.05 is 1 − 0.95^k; Bonferroni uses 0.05/k per test.

cards.front: Unit of analysis in a pilot
cards.back: Animals, not technical readings, are the independent units; readings improve precision of each animal but do not add animals.
n per group = 2 (z_α/2 + z_β)² (σ_b² + σ_t²/m) / δ²; beyond about three readings, more readings per animal barely help.
It supplies variance estimates and a hypothesis. The selected effect is inflated; plan from the smallest effect of interest and pre-specify one primary outcome.
P(D|H) is the probability of the observed data under a candidate state; it is not P(H|D).
P(Hᵢ|D)=P(D|Hᵢ)P(Hᵢ)/ΣⱼP(D|Hⱼ)P(Hⱼ). The denominator is model evidence.
Average future-outcome probabilities over the posterior; compare a forecast only with data kept separate from fitting.
A p-value conditions on a fixed null. A posterior probability conditions on observed data and a stated prior over hypotheses or parameters.
With θ ~ Beta(α,β), s successes and f failures give θ|D ~ Beta(α+s,β+f).
For Beta(a,b), E[θ]=a/(a+b); the mean is a summary, not the whole posterior.
Integrate future binomial probabilities over the Beta posterior; uncertainty in a shared θ changes multi-trial predictive probabilities.
The basic model assumes a prespecified prior and conditionally exchangeable Bernoulli outcomes with one common rate; covariates and batch effects are absent.

cards.front: What must agree in a confirmatory protocol’s unit definitions?
cards.back: The randomization unit, independent sampling unit and sample-size calculation must match the analysis model. Technical repeats need their own within-unit role.

cards.front: What separates a predeclared primary question from an exploratory choice?
cards.back: The primary outcome, timepoint, contrast and analysis are fixed before new outcomes exist. A pilot-selected marker can motivate that question but cannot retroactively become pre-specified.

cards.front: Why round the retained-unit requirement up before applying attrition allowance?
cards.back: The retained analysis target is a discrete count. After that target is fixed, divide by the planned retention fraction and round the allocation count up again.

cards.front: What extra assumption is needed for 1−(1−alpha)^m but not the Bonferroni bound?
cards.back: Independence of the tests gives the product probability. The union bound behind Bonferroni controls the family-wise probability without that assumption.

cards.front: What information must survive a tidy table and plot?
cards.back: Unit identity, arm, time, outcome scale, technical-replicate identity, denominators and documented missingness/exclusions must remain distinguishable.

cards.front: What must precede a joint-density moment calculation?
cards.back: The support and normalization, followed by the correct marginal or joint integral; arbitrary rectangular bounds can include impossible pairs.
It establishes a zero centered product expectation under finite moments, not factorization of the entire joint law.

cards.front: Why distinguish marginal and conditional reference sets?
cards.back: Conditioning changes the distribution and its support; the unconditional average cannot be reused automatically for a fixed predictor.

cards.front: How should total-variance terms be interpreted?
cards.back: First as within-condition and between-conditional-mean variation in the declared model; scientific labels require an appropriate data-generating explanation.

cards.front: How does independent right censoring enter this exponential likelihood?
cards.back: Each censored duration contributes survival exposure, while only observed events contribute a rate factor.

cards.front: What does likelihood curvature fail to establish by itself?
cards.back: It does not verify finite-sample interval coverage, the censoring assumptions or fit of the event-time model.

cards.front: Why state a parameter space before optimization?
cards.back: An interior stationary point, an attained boundary maximum and an unattained supremum are different mathematical conclusions.

cards.front: How do likelihood and posterior differ?
cards.back: Likelihood compares parameter values through fixed observations; a posterior additionally uses a prior and normalizes over the declared parameter space.

cards.front: Which quantities add in normal conjugacy?
cards.back: Independent likelihood precision and prior precision add; variances or standard deviations do not add in that posterior formula.

cards.front: Why is a predictive interval wider than the posterior interval for a mean?
cards.back: It includes new observation variability in addition to current uncertainty about the shared mean.

cards.front: Can conditional independence coexist with marginal dependence?
cards.back: Yes. Integrating over a shared uncertain parameter can induce dependence between quantities that are independent when that parameter is fixed.

cards.front: What does a credible-interval probability depend on?
cards.back: The stated prior, sampling likelihood, observations and interval rule; it is not automatically a frequentist coverage guarantee or empirical model validation.

cards.front: What must a reproducible regression fit retain?
cards.back: Raw rows, design columns/rank, coefficient solution, residuals and target assumptions; a coefficient list alone does not identify the analysis.

cards.front: Why can a slope change after adjustment?
cards.back: Correlated predictors can share projected response variation; changing the model changes the conditional comparison and may alter the slope without establishing causality.

cards.front: Why does fitted rank matter for a residual variance estimate?
cards.back: The projection removes as many independent directions as the design rank; the remaining residual dimension determines the usual mean-square denominator.

cards.front: Which target requires a new-error contribution?
cards.back: Prediction of a new noisy observation, rather than estimation of the model mean at specified predictors.

cards.front: Why is a binomial variance wrong for these draws?
cards.back: Sampling without replacement makes the indicators dependent; the covariance term changes the variance even though each marginal success probability is the same.

cards.front: How can conditional computations be independently checked?
cards.back: Derive and normalize the conditional density, then compare its moment with a direct joint/marginal calculation on the same support.

cards.front: What does a procedure name fail to guarantee?
cards.back: Nominal confidence and a bootstrap label do not establish finite-sample coverage; evaluate the actual sampling procedure, especially at boundaries.

cards.front: Which experiment gives this exact p-value its denominator?
cards.back: The specified randomized allocations of fixed sharp-null outcomes; an arbitrary observational regrouping need not have that reference distribution.

cards.front: What distinguishes a projection check from model validation?
cards.back: Residual orthogonality verifies the least-squares algebra; independence, variance, design and empirical mean-model adequacy require other evidence.

cards.front: Why state the target and design alongside a prediction?
cards.back: The new-observation noise term and interpretation depend on what is predicted and how units/data were generated, not only on fitted coefficients.

cards.front: Which ledgers must a censored likelihood report preserve?
cards.back: Observed duration and event status separately, total exposure, event count, parameter domain, units and the censoring mechanism assumption.

cards.front: What should a cumulative inference report distinguish?
cards.back: Sampling estimates/coverage, likelihood, posterior probability and future prediction, with each tied to its own parameter, unit, design and assumptions.
(a × d)/(b × c); close to the risk ratio only when the outcome is rare.
Row total × column total ÷ grand total; χ² needs expected counts of about 5 or more.
Conditions on the margins; the hypergeometric distribution gives the exact p-value for small tables.
An association reverses when a confounder is pooled over; stratify or use the Mantel–Haenszel estimate.
F = MS_B/MS_W on k − 1 and N − k degrees of freedom; near 1 when all means are equal.
SS_B/SS_total: the share of variation between groups.
Use pooled MS_W with Bonferroni or Tukey adjustment, or comparisons planned in advance.
SS_B = Σnⱼ(ȳⱼ − ȳ)²; SS_W = Σ(nⱼ − 1)sⱼ².
